bigPicture.subtitle: The Lamb on the Throne Is Making All Things New
bigPicture.thesis: If we had to summarize the Book of Revelation in one overarching thought, it is this: behind the turmoil of history stands the throne of God, and on that throne is the Lamb who was slain; He holds the scroll of history, He has already overcome the dragon by His blood, and He is coming soon to judge every evil, to bring down Babylon and the beast, and to make all things new — so His people must worship God alone and overcome as He did, by faithful witness even to death.
paragraphs: Revelation was written to seven small churches in a vast empire. Some were persecuted, some compromised, some asleep, some lukewarm. The empire looked eternal; its emperor was worshipped as lord and god; its wealth and power seemed unstoppable. Into that world the risen Jesus sent a letter — an unveiling — that showed what was really happening.

First, He showed Himself: the Son of Man among the lampstands, with eyes like fire and the keys of death in His hand (ch. 1). Then He spoke to each church with perfect knowledge, calling them to repent and promising extravagant rewards to those who overcome (chs. 2–3). Then John was taken up to the throne room of heaven, where God reigns and the slain Lamb takes the scroll of history (chs. 4–5).

From the throne flow the judgements — seals, trumpets and bowls — growing in intensity, each a warning and a call to repentance (chs. 6–16). Behind them John saw the deeper conflict: the dragon, the beast and the false prophet against the woman, the Lamb and His witnesses (chs. 12–14). He saw the great prostitute Babylon in all her glamour, and her sudden fall (chs. 17–18). He saw heaven explode in Hallelujahs, the marriage of the Lamb, and the Rider called Faithful and True defeat every enemy by the sword of His mouth (ch. 19). He saw Satan bound and finally destroyed, and every person standing before the great white throne (ch. 20).

And at the end he saw what all of it was for: a new heaven and a new earth, the holy city coming down like a bride, God dwelling with His people, every tear wiped away, the river of life and the tree of life, and the servants of God seeing His face (chs. 21–22). The last words are an invitation and a prayer: ‘Come.’ ‘Amen! Yes, come, Lord Jesus.’ The book that seems so full of terror is, in the end, the book of the Bible's greatest hope.

map.intro: Revelation is the twenty-seventh and last book of the New Testament, and the last book of the Bible. It gathers up the threads of the whole story — creation, fall, Israel, the prophets, the Gospel — and ties them together in the victory of the Lamb and the renewal of all things.

sections.title: The End That Answers the Beginning
sections.body: Revelation is the Bible's final chapter, and it deliberately mirrors the first. Genesis opens with the heavens and the earth; Revelation with a new heaven and a new earth. Genesis has a garden, a river and the tree of life; Revelation a garden-city, the river of life and the tree of life open to all. Genesis brings the serpent, the curse and death; Revelation the serpent thrown down, ‘no curse any more’ and ‘death will be no more’. In Genesis humanity is driven from God's presence; in Revelation ‘God’s dwelling is with people’ and ‘they will see his face’. And the Babylon that began at Babel ends in fire, replaced by the city of God.

sections.title: How This Study Has Read Revelation
sections.body: Christians have read Revelation in four main ways: as mostly fulfilled in the first centuries, as a map of church history, as mainly about the final events before Christ's return, or as a timeless picture of the battle between Christ and evil. This study has read each passage in the way its own words suggest: Revelation spoke first to seven real churches under Rome; it describes realities that recur in every age; and it looks forward to a real, personal return of Christ, a final judgement and a new creation. It speaks in symbols drawn from the Old Testament — and often tells us so (1:20; 11:8; 17:9, 18).

sections.title: Hard Passages Read Honestly
sections.body: Several passages divide faithful readers. The 144,000 and the great multitude (ch. 7) are read by some as two groups, by others (as here) as one people seen two ways. The two witnesses (ch. 11) may be two end-time prophets or the witnessing church. The woman of chapter 12 is the people of God from whom the Messiah came, and Christians have also seen Mary in her. The beast and 666 (ch. 13) pointed John's readers to Nero and Rome, and also to every power that claims divine honour. Babylon (chs. 17–18) was Rome, and is every civilisation built on idolatry, greed and the blood of God's people. The thousand years (ch. 20) is read in three main ways — premillennial, amillennial and postmillennial — and this study has set them out without pretending the question is closed. What all agree on is the book's centre: the Lamb wins, and His people with Him.

sections.title: Word Families in Revelation
sections.body: Revelation added eight new families to the study: witness (μάρτυς, μαρτυρία, μαρτύριον, μαρτυρέω — the faithful witness who becomes a ‘martyr’); crown (στέφανος, the victor's wreath, against διάδημα, the royal crown claimed by the dragon and worn ‘many’ by Christ); book (βίβλος, βιβλίον, βιβλαρίδιον); lamb (ἀρνίον, Revelation's name for Christ, against ἀμνός and ἀρήν); wrath (ὀργή, settled anger, against θυμός, anger as passion, often side by side); sword (ῥομφαία from Christ's mouth against the beast's μάχαιρα); judge (κρίνω, κρίσις the act, κρίμα the verdict); and holy (ἅγιος, set apart, against ὅσιος, ‘you only are holy’). Familiar families recurred everywhere: καιρός and χρόνος in time, δύναμις, ἐξουσία, κράτος and ἰσχύς in power, and the four time-words of 9:15 — hour, day, month and year — in a single phrase.

roadAhead.intro: The Road Ahead: Revelation is the last book of the Bible, so the road ahead turns back to the beginning. The best way to understand Revelation's ending is to read the Bible's opening. The next two books are Genesis, the book of beginnings, which Revelation brings to completion; and Exodus, the story of redemption, whose plagues, Passover lamb, song by the sea and tabernacle shape Revelation on almost every page. (Genesis and Exodus are not yet in this app's Bible text, so they are described here in our own words.)

books.connection: Genesis is where every thread of Revelation begins. God creates the heavens and the earth and calls them good; He plants a garden with a river and the tree of life, and walks with the man and woman He made in His image. Then the serpent deceives, sin enters, the ground is cursed, death comes, and the way to the tree of life is guarded by cherubim with a flaming sword. God promises that the woman's offspring will crush the serpent's head. Humanity builds Babel to make a name for itself, and God scatters it. And God calls Abraham, promising that through him all the families of the earth will be blessed, and that his descendants will be as countless as the stars. Watch for each of these as you read: Revelation is Genesis answered — the serpent crushed, the curse lifted, Babylon fallen, the tree of life open, and a countless multitude from every nation blessed through Abraham's offspring, the Lamb.

Exodus gave Revelation its pictures of judgement and redemption. God hears His people crying under Pharaoh's oppression and sends plagues — water to blood, frogs, boils, hail, locusts, darkness — while Pharaoh hardens his heart. On the night of Passover, the blood of a lamb shelters God's people from judgement. They pass through the sea, and on the far shore Moses and Miriam sing of God's victory. At Sinai, with thunder, lightning, smoke and trumpet blast, God makes them ‘a kingdom of priests’, and He comes to dwell among them in the tabernacle, which His glory fills. Watch for each of these as you read: the trumpets and bowls of Revelation are the plagues on a world scale; the Lamb is the true Passover; the victors sing the song of Moses and the Lamb; and the tabernacle becomes the new Jerusalem, where God dwells with His people forever.

themesMastered.title: Jesus, the First and the Last
themesMastered.body: Revelation is first ‘the Revelation of Jesus Christ’. He is the faithful witness, the firstborn of the dead, the ruler of the kings of the earth, who walks among His churches with eyes like fire: “I am the first and the last, and the Living one. I was dead, and behold, I am alive forever and ever” (Revelation 1:17–18). At the end He claims every title of God: “I am the Alpha and the Omega, the First and the Last, the Beginning and the End” (Revelation 22:13).

themesMastered.title: Overcome: Christ's Word to the Churches
themesMastered.body: Jesus knows every church — its love, its compromise, its suffering, its sleep, its lukewarmness — and calls each to repent or hold fast. Every letter ends with a promise to the one who overcomes, and the greatest is the last: “He who overcomes, I will give to him to sit down with me on my throne, as I also overcame, and sat down with my Father on his throne” (Revelation 3:21).

themesMastered.title: The Throne and the Lamb
themesMastered.body: Behind all of history stands a throne, and it is not empty: “Holy, holy, holy is the Lord God, the Almighty, who was and who is and who is to come!” (Revelation 4:8). At its centre is “a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain” (Revelation 5:6). God's power is revealed in the cross. The Lamb alone is worthy to open the scroll of history, because He “bought us for God with your blood, out of every tribe, language, people, and nation” (Revelation 5:9).

themesMastered.title: Judgements That Call to Repentance
themesMastered.body: The seals, trumpets and bowls show God's just judgements on a world in rebellion, released by the Lamb, limited by God, and answering the prayers of His suffering people. Yet again and again “They didn’t repent” (Revelation 9:20). Judgement alone does not change hearts; the witness of God's people does (11:13). And heaven confesses, “Yes, Lord God, the Almighty, true and righteous are your judgments” (Revelation 16:7).

themesMastered.title: The War Behind History
themesMastered.body: The dragon, the beast and the false prophet wage war on God's people, demanding worship and controlling the marketplace. But the dragon has already been thrown down by the cross, and “They overcame him because of the Lamb’s blood, and because of the word of their testimony. They didn’t love their life, even to death” (Revelation 12:11). The beast's power is ‘given’ and limited; “Here is the endurance and the faith of the saints” (Revelation 13:10).

themesMastered.title: Come Out of Babylon
themesMastered.body: Babylon the great — the world-system of wealth, pleasure, power and idolatry, drunk on the blood of the saints — looks glorious but is already judged. Her fall comes in one hour. God's call to His people is urgent: “Come out of her, my people, that you have no participation in her sins, and that you don’t receive of her plagues” (Revelation 18:4).

themesMastered.title: All Things New
themesMastered.body: Christ returns as King of kings and defeats every enemy; Satan, death and Hades are destroyed; every person is judged. Then God makes all things new: “Behold, God’s dwelling is with people, and he will dwell with them, and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God. He will wipe away every tear from their eyes” (Revelation 21:3–4). And His servants “will see his face” (Revelation 22:4).

experientialLesson.intro: How do you walk out the Book of Revelation practically moving forward? Here is your experiential blueprint:

steps.title: Begin Every Day at the Throne
steps.lesson: The Lesson: “After these things I looked and saw a door opened in heaven, and the first voice that I heard, like a trumpet speaking with me, was one saying, ‘Come up here, and I will show you the things which must happen after this’” (Revelation 4:1).
steps.practice: The Practice: For the next month, before you check the news or your phone, read one hymn of worship from Revelation (4:8, 4:11, 5:9–10, 5:12–13, 7:10–12, 11:15–18, 15:3–4, 19:1–8) and pray it aloud. Then bring the day's fears and tasks to the One on the throne. Let worship, not worry, set the tone of your day.

steps.title: Overcome as the Lamb Overcame
steps.lesson: The Lesson: “They overcame him because of the Lamb’s blood, and because of the word of their testimony. They didn’t love their life, even to death” (Revelation 12:11).
steps.practice: The Practice: Read the seven letters (chs. 2–3) and ask which church you most resemble. Write down one thing Jesus would praise and one thing He would correct. Then take three concrete steps this month: confess and repent of the compromise He names; share your testimony with one person; and choose one costly act of faithfulness — giving, forgiving, refusing a compromise at work — that shows you love Him more than your own comfort.

steps.title: Come Out of Babylon and Say ‘Come’
steps.lesson: The Lesson: “The Spirit and the bride say, ‘Come!’ He who hears, let him say, ‘Come!’ He who is thirsty, let him come. He who desires, let him take the water of life freely” (Revelation 22:17).
steps.practice: The Practice: Identify one way Babylon's values have a hold on you — in spending, entertainment, ambition or comfort — and take a clear step to come out of it. Then pray daily for three people who do not yet know Jesus, and invite at least one of them this month to ‘come and drink’. End each day with the Bible's last prayer: ‘Amen. Come, Lord Jesus.’

finalDeclaration: “Lord Jesus Christ, I declare that You are the faithful witness, the firstborn of the dead and the ruler of the kings of the earth. You love me, You freed me from my sins by Your blood, and You made me part of Your kingdom and a priest to Your God and Father. To You be the glory and the dominion forever and ever. You walk among Your churches with eyes like fire; I invite You to search me, and I will repent where You show me, and hold fast what is good. I declare that the throne of heaven is occupied, and that the Lord God Almighty reigns. Holy, holy, holy is He. I declare that You, the Lamb who was slain, are worthy to take the scroll of history, for You bought me and people from every nation with Your blood. I will not fear the dragon, for he has been thrown down; I will overcome him by Your blood and by the word of my testimony, and I will not love my life more than You. I refuse the mark of the beast and the wine of Babylon; I will come out of her and keep myself for You, my Bridegroom. I declare that Your judgements are true and righteous, and that every wrong will be put right. I believe You are coming soon as King of kings and Lord of lords, that death will be destroyed, and that my name is written in the Lamb's book of life by Your grace alone. I look for a new heaven and a new earth, for the city where God dwells with His people, where every tear is wiped away and there is no more curse. I will see Your face. Until then I will worship God alone, keep the words of this book, and say to every thirsty soul, ‘Come, and take the water of life freely.’ Amen. Come, Lord Jesus. The grace of the Lord Jesus be with all the saints. Amen!”
